messages.subject: D5 MRDS
messages.body_plain:
Hello

=20

I am just beginning to use the D5 MRDS engine and I must congratulate =
the developers on bringing us yet another improvement on this great =
software package.

=20

I have 2 questions:

=20

I am analyzing a series of surveys, only the last of which was done with =
double observers. For comparability, I have analyzed them all as single =
platform surveys, but it is of interest to get a g(0) estimate for the =
last survey, with an associated measure of variance. In the D5 output, =
the point estimates for p(0) are given but the variance is not =
immediately obvious to me. Is it the se of the intercept term in the =
conditional detection function? (sorry if this is an obvious question).

=20

Secondly, I am analyzing a survey that was done in Buckland-Turnock (BT) =
mode, where the secondary platform was aware of the sightings of the =
primary platform, but the primary was not aware of the sightings of the =
secondary. As I understand it the secondary only registered a sighting =
if they made it first. Therefore, if they heard the primary make a =
sighting they had not yet seen, they would not register it themselves. =
It seems to me that this survey should be analyzed in trial =
configuration because there is only one-way independence. But I was =
wondering what the ramifications would be of analyzing in independent =
observer mode? I ask this because it is of interest to get an estimate =
of g(0) for the combined platforms, which is not possible with the trial =
mode. I cannot think why the estimate of p(0) for the combined observers =
would not be valid.

=20

I appreciate any help I can get. Many thanks,

=20

Daniel Pike

Fax: +47 77 75 01 81

danie...@nammco.no

=20

See us on the Web at www.nammco.no <http://www.nammco.no>.

=20

messages.body_plain:
I am using Distance4.1 w/ a relatively simple (but large)10-min
point count dataset.  Our study areas are arranged into transects and
pts. w/ each point in a specific habitat and each bird observation
recorded w/ an approximate distance.   I want to make some comparisons
across areas/habitats/species using distance estimates and have figured
out the software for the most part.  I have received some advise/done
some research and decided an estimate per point is appropriate even
though some are using a small sample size to get the estimate...........

My question is regarding the model definition.  I was hoping to get some
advice on what is appropriate for this type of analysis?  I've played
around w/ the various options and get quite a bit of variance in the
density estimates?  Should I just go w/ the default?  I've found papers
where the researchers have used Distance for their analyses, but haven't
found specifics on what inputs were used?

I'd appreciate any advice.

Bonnie Hunt

Daniel:
Q1: This was an oversight on my part in not including an se for g(0) (or=20
what we call p(0) in the output) because I had not envisioned it being=20
used as you'ld like.  I'll be going through the code in the next couple=20
of weeks tidying up loose ends for a final release and will output the=20
se.  In the time being you can compute it yourself if the model is=20
simple.  You are on the right track but it will depend on the model you=20
used for the conditional detection function.  If you have only distance=20
in the conditional det fct model then the se of the intercept is the=20
correct value to use except that you need to translate it to p(0). =20
However, if you ever other covariates which you are likely to have then=20
you won't have all the information you need to compute it.  I think I'll=20
change this to ouput the v-c matrix for the parameters so any variance=20
can be computed.=20

Q2: If the data are set up as IO in the way that you described then all=20
of the trials for the secondary observer will be seen because the=20
secondary will have "seen" all the primary sightings, so the result will=20
be that p(0) for the secondary observer will be 1 so the pooled p(0)=20
will be 1, which is not what you are looking for presumably.  I'm=20
somewhat guessing what you are looking for so maybe you can send a=20
message directly to me that describes the setup in more detail.  If I=20
think it is useful for the list I'll cc the list as well with my=20
response.  If what you want is p(0) for both teams combined assuming=20
that p(0) is the same for both teams, then it would be=20
p_both(0)=3D2*p(0)-p(0)^2

regards  --jeff

messages.subject: Running Distance under Linux or Mac
messages.subject_clean: Running Distance under Linux or Mac
messages.body_plain:
Distance-sampling list:

In response to a user question, I have updated the section of the Distance
support page that deals with how to run Distance from other operating systems
(a copy below, without all the hyperlinks).  Also, Distance 5 includes a
library for the free, multiplatform software R that fits single and double
observer distance sampling data (but without adjustment terms for the single-
platform detection function at present).  Although this library has only been
tested in R for Windows, it may well run under other operating systems
(possibly with some minor tweaking - let us know if you try it).

If anyone has any more information to contribute on this topic, please email
me!  Thanks,

 - Len Thomas

Linux: Although we don't have any direct experience, Distance should run
without problems within the emulation software VMWare or win4lin.  For VMWare,
note that there is a free version called VMWare player, and if you search the
web under something like "Free VMWare" you will find instructions about how to
set up operating system images using free software (one site is
http://johnbokma.com/vmware-player/).  Other possibilities are to use the free
emulators Bochs (pronounced "box" - slow, apparently) or QEMU (with the
accelerator module).  For up to date information, try searching the web for
"PC Emulators" or "PC Virtualizers".  If you try any of these solutions,
please let us know how you get on!

Apple Macintosh: Distance 3.5 and Distance 4.0 were tested on a G4 PowerMac
running Virtual PC (since acquired by Microsoft) and both ran without
problems, although both run quite slowly and Distance 4 especially needs quite
a bit of memory.  Other emulators will probably work as well - see
http://www.macwindows.com/emulator.html for a list and latest news.  If you
try any, then let us know how they work.

--

messages.subject: Trapping webs: multipliers and right-truncation
messages.body_plain:
I have a pair of concerns regarding trapping webs and was hoping someone =
out there could shed some light on the subject.  I ran a number of webs =
in a burned ponderosa pine forest on salvage logged and non-logged =
treatments.  Peromyscus species comprised the bulk of the captures.

1)  Captures consistantly increased with distance from the web's center. =
 As a result, the detection functions fit to the data produce denstiy =
estimates lower than what was observed.  Right-truncation works to a =
degree, but not without producing very large confidence intervals and =
greater CV values.  Left-truncation drives the estimate down further.
     Is this a common problem with trapping webs and how is it dealt =
with?

2)  Mark-recapture data showed that the g(0)=3D1 assumption was met with =
varying success.  That is, I oftern had new individuals appearing on the =
last day of trapping (4 trap nights).  The users guide for program =
DISTANCE suggests dividing the density estimate by the observed g(0) in =
these cases.  I have ideas on how to calculate a value for g(0), but =
wanted to hear how other people have approached this issue first.

If you have any suggestions, or need more background, please refer to my =
e-mail at:
krwi...@stcloudstat.edu

Thanks for your time!

messages.subject: Re: Trapping webs: multipliers and right-truncation
messages.body_plain:
Bill/List:

Trapping webs do present some inherent difficulties.  Truncation does
offer some help, but recognize that truncation is a reduction of data,
and any reduction in data will result in concomitant reduction in precision.

For particularly vagile species, Clethrionomys in my experience, and I
would not be surprised if Peromyscus are similar; many animals encounter
traps in the outer rings because the area sampled by the outer rings of
a web is large relative to inner rings.  Hence truncation of the outer
rings is common.  See Section 6.8.5 of Buckland et al. (2001:221) for an
example dealing with Peromyscus, where right truncation was employed.

The use of left-truncation for point transect data (of which trapping
webs are a special case) is not recommended, as it is critical that you
produce estimates of h(0) which is the derivative of the detection
function at the centre of the web; you need all the information you can
get near the centre of the web, tossing some of it is a poor idea.

Finally with regard to adjusting for g(0)<1.  Having new individuals
entering your sample near the end of a trapping session is not
necessarily an indication of g(0)<1, an alternative explanation is that
your population is not closed for 4 days, and hence D-hat is changing
during your study.  Recognize that estimating g(0) requires not only a
point estimate, but also an estimate of the precision with which you
have estimated g(0).  So you cannot rely on an ad hoc method of
estimating g(0), but rather would need a method capable of producing a
measure of precision as well.

In summary consult the worked example in Buckland et al. (2001) that
references data from Anderson et al. (1983) on the same species as your
study organism.

messages.subject_clean: Grouping replicates to increase sample size
messages.body_plain:
I am surveying small carnivores in Mongolia using line transects and
spotlighting from a truck and am new to Distance surveys. I have low
sample sizes and would like to group seasonal replicates to increase
sample size. I carry out a 56km transect consisting of 8 separate line
transects every week, producing 12-13 weekly samples per 3 month
season. Can I group data per season to increase sample sizes, for
example I generally see 5 corsac foxes per survey, can I use the data
from all 13 surveys per season (roughly 60-65 sightings) to estimate
density? Does anyone have any advice about this issue.

Steve Ross

messages.subject: Re: Grouping replicates to increase sample size
messages.subject_clean: Grouping replicates to increase sample size
messages.body_plain:
Hi Steve, list,

Enter the data into distance as 8 samples (lines) each of length (line
length*number of visits).    So, for a 7km line visited 12 times in a season,
enter this as a 84km line.  All the observations for that line go in the
observation layer, as if you had surveyed an 84km line once.  Otherwise, the
analysis proceeds as usual.

Note that 8 is a rather small sample size of lines.  You would be better to do
fewer temporal replicates over more lines - especially since in your habitat,
which I guess is Mongolian plains, it's relatively easy to drive where you
like.  You really want at least 20-30 - but if it is equally easy to sample a
new line as it is to drive down an old one, then do a new line each time.  If
you sample 96 lines is a 3-month season, then a good design would be a
systematic grid of 96 7km lines placed throughout your study area - see
Advanced Distance Sampling figure 7.8 for an example.  This kind of design can
be created using the survey design module in Distance.  Another good design is
a circuit design, where the transect is (say) a square (see Fig 7.3 of
Introduction to Distance sampling).  That way you can start at any convenient
point on the square, and you end up where you started.  Disadvantages of this
design are: (i) you may chase animals away from the start point, so get a
biased sample as you come back to it at the end of the survey, or you may move
animals around the square ahead of you; (ii) such designs can't be created
(yet) in Distance -- although you could always generate a systematic grid of
points in Distance and then superimpose the squares on a map by hand.

If you do create many more lines, you'll probably want to visit them in a
systematic manner if possible, to guard against any large-scale movement of
animals through the study area within the 3 month season.  So (if logistically
possible -- ie study area not too large) you might visit lines 1, 9, 17, ...
first, then lines 2, 10, 18, ... etc etc.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

> >From: "Distance Development" <dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>

Firstly, your specific question about the model definition options.  The
Introduction to Distance Sampling book contains detailed discussions of
general analysis strategy (section 2.5), example analysis of simulated point
transect data (starting at 5.2) and real data (8.6 and 8.7).  The analysis
strategy is also more-or-less copied in the online manual ("CDS Analysis
Guidelines"), and one very relevant sentence is "We have steered clear of
defining specific 'cookbook' procedures for data analysis and, above all,
recommend that you do not unthinkingly use the Distance defaults."

I agree that we don't have a step-by-step example of the analysis of point
transect data using Distance e.g., in the manual, but hopefully the above
can help you formulate a suitable strategy, along with your other reading. I
get the feeling that there's a lot of grey literature out there that gives
specific advice, so perhaps others could post you information about any of
this they know of and you could summarize back to the list?

Other points that occured to me:

- 10 minute counts will tend to overestimate abundance.  See the recent
paper by Buckland in press in Auk ("Point transect surveys for songbirds:
robust methodlogies"), available from http://www.creem.st-
and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf <http://and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf>

- A common strategy to look for, e.g., habitat effects on density, is to
predict density by point using Distance and then do a separate regression of
habitat (and other covariates) on density.  There are lots of issues here,
for example (i) density estimates are not independent between points due to
fitting a pooled detection function (even if MCDS is used); (ii) how should
each density estiamte be weighted if they differ in the estimation
uncertainty; etc.  I think these have been discussed previously - try
searching the list for "spatial model" or "density surface" (possibly also
"bootstrap".

- In your case, with points nested within transects, you may want to
consider a hierarchical model, if you are using the modelling approach
outlined above.

Hope this helps some,

 - Len

A couple more things occured to me in reviewing this:

- if you're estimating density by sample (point) then the encounter rate
part of the variance will be assuming that the distribution of counts is
Poisson, since it can't use the usual empirical variance estiamte (formula
3.77 of the Intro book).  This is unlikely to be reliable.  Whether you're
interested in a reliable estimate of density by point depends on the
ultimate goals of the analysis -- in the two step process outlined above
it's not that important.

- in general, especially if you're using MCDS, I'd recommend using the beta
of Distance 5 rather than Distance 4.1.  However, if you're just using the
CDS engine then Distance 4.1 is fine.

Cheers,

 - Len

messages.subject: problem with stratum categories
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

=20

I have done point bird surveys in 6 vegetation types (155 points in
total, most surveys were repeated 6 days in the same points, but some
were repeated only 3 days), and I would like to estimate densities in
each one of the vegetation types, but I am running into a weird problem.
Each time I import the data from a text file, instead of 6 categories,
the program generates 32. I tried simplifying the data by importing only
vegetation type (as a region), point id (as sample), and the distance
records (observation), and effort (sample), and changing the names of
those vegetation types to level numbers instead of text. But the program
still generates 32 categories when it comes to calculate density by
stratum (using the regular CDS estimation with vegetation type as
stratum). In other words, I get more than one estimate for vegetation
type 1, more than one estimate for veg type 2, etc., and they are all
different! I don't know what else to try and don't understand what is
going on. Does anyone have any suggestion? Any comments will be
appreciated. Thanks,

=20

Christine

=20

Christine N. Meynard

PhD Candidate, Graduate Group in Ecology

Dept. Env. Sci. & Policy

University of California, Davis

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

=20

Yesterday I asked about why Distance would generate more than one
category for each level of a factor (vegetation type). It turns out that
the factors have to be sorted and grouped, otherwise the program
recognizes each new group as a new level. Thanks to the people who
replied to my inquiry. So this brings me to another question. What if I
want to use two factors as a covariate in an analysis?  Let's say for
example that I have 6 vegetation types and 3 forest stages
(early-successional, mid-successional, and old-growth). These factors
are not fully nested because each vegetation type may have
representation in several or all successional stages, and vice versa. So
when I sort the data by vegetation type the forest stages will be
unsorted and vice-versa. Does this mean that I cannot have two factors
as covariates in an analysis?=20

=20

Thanks for your input,

=20

Christine

messages.subject: Re: another question about factors
messages.body_plain:
Christine-

Not sure where you are going with this.  Are your factors really strata
for which you want to estimate density?  That is different than using a
factor variable in the model for detection probability.  Distance is not
particularly sophisticated with it's handling of designs because its
original intent was simply to estimate abundance/density rather than as
a tool to investigate relationships between density and ecological
factors or for experimental design.  Clearly, this has become a drawback
because it is a natural evolution of thought and analysis.
Unfortunately, the software is lagging and it is something we are trying
to correct.

If your goal is to estimate density for a set of vegetation x forest
stages and these can be represented as discrete regions, then I would
suggest that you create a variable you could call strata which would
have has its value the possible pairings of vegetation and forest
stages.  If you then sorted by strata and then lines/points within
strata, it should work fine.  You can keep the forest stage and
vegetation as factor variables for modelling detection probability.  If
your forest stage-vegetation data don't represent specific regions that
you sampled but each line/point is in a forest/vegetation type you are
still okay but you'll only want to compare densities and NOT estimate
abundance for each strata.  If you have line transect data and each
observation has a forest/veg type you are currently out of luck but in
the upcoming D6 it will contain a spatial modelling component.  Len/Eric
may have more to add here when they get time.

--jeff
